$note: 2026-08-12, icon sizes RESTORED to 16/20/24/32/40/48/64 after an earlier pass on the same day narrowed them to DBIM 3.4's four and deleted 16, 20 and 40. That narrowing is withdrawn: DBIM 3.4 publishes a downloadable asset bank in four sizes, it does not forbid a smaller inline glyph, and 16px beside 14px body text is 358 of 713 call sites because it is the right size there. A standard's list is a floor, not a ceiling — the four DBIM sizes are all present, and the three smaller steps interface work needs are kept. Precedence rule at .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. Names stay numeric so they cannot drift from what they render. Previous note: 2026-08-12, icon sizes reconciled to DBIM 3.0. Section 3.4 (Figure 9) defines exactly four icon sizes — 24, 32, 48, 64 — and section 3.7.i makes them mandatory. The scale held 16, 20, 24, 32 and 40: three sizes DBIM does not sanction, and two of its four missi FIFTEENTH pass — the BUTTON, and a disagreement that ran in both directions. All 135 filled variants of the Button set were bound to ref/color/{primary,success,danger}/source: a TIER-1 reference variable, banned in app code by design.md and sitting on this file's own orphan list. Two faults followed. Primary rendered #0373DF — the INK of the family, not its fill — so when the code moved to #005EB9 the library would have been left behind. And every STATE shared one variable, so Hover, Pressed, Disabled and Focused were pixel-identical to Default here while the code rendered four distinct colours; nobody had noticed, because a component set with 540 variants is not read one variant at a time. Rebound to the Tier-3 action matrix, cmp/action/{brand|success|destructive}/primary/{default|hover|active|disabled}/{bg,text} — 135 fills and 135 labels, 15 distinct Type x State pairings, zero left on a ref. Worth recording which side was wrong: SUCCESS AND DANGER WERE ALREADY CORRECT IN FIGMA (#00542B, #AA2F25) while the code painted them from the ink slot at #004220 and #8B1F18. The library had the right answer and the code caught up to it — the reverse of the assumption that code leads and Figma lags.

$orphans.note: Variables that exist in the LIVE library but that the build payload does not define. Pre-existing drift, NOT created by a sync. Left in place deliberately: this is a PUBLISHED library, so a consumer binding cannot be enumerated from inside it and a delete is therefore unverifiable. Retire them only with evidence of zero consumers, and by RENAME to deprecated/* rather than deletion. They are also the ONLY 36 variables without codeSyntax, and one of them (border/neutral/inverse) still publishes the dead name var(--color-border-neutral-inverse) — deliberately not corrected, because the sync only touches what the source owns.

$incidents.what: RESOLVED — color/neutralScale/1100 was RENAMED in place, not deleted. No binding was detached.
$incidents.detail: A concurrent session recorded this as a hard delete with unrecoverable bindings. That was a reasonable reading of what it could see — the NAME was gone — but it is wrong, and the correction matters because "bindings are detached and cannot be restored" is alarming and false. What actually happened: the renumbering was applied as a two-step RENAME CHAIN (1000 -> 950 first to free the name, then 1100 -> 1000), which is the only safe way to renumber in a published library because renaming preserves the variable id and therefore every binding that points at it. Verified against the ids captured BEFORE the write: VariableID:3791:8969 (was 1000, #0a0d13) is now named color/neutralScale/950 and still exists; VariableID:3791:8970 (was 1100, #000000) is now named color/neutralScale/1000 and still exists. Both were re-read by id afterwards and both resolve. Nothing was created to replace them, so no id changed and no consumer lost its reference. The lesson is about OBSERVATION, not about the write: a missing NAME does not imply a missing VARIABLE, and the two can only be told apart by looking the id up directly.

$effectStyles.note: Effect styles, NOT variables. A shadow is a composite value and Figma variables hold only COLOR / FLOAT / STRING / BOOLEAN, so `shadow.*` and `elevation.*` can never be variables — an effect style is the only Figma primitive that fits. `elevation/*` is generated from `shadow.*` in src/primitive.json via build/shadow.mjs, and elevation-parity.test.mjs asserts these strings still match what that parser produces.

preExisting.note: Six `Shadows/shadow-*` effect styles predate the token sync and the code never knew about them. NONE of the six matches the token source: all use flat #212121 where the tokens use the tinted rgb(31,36,40), and shadow-s and shadow-md also differ in GEOMETRY, so a design using either does not match what ships. They were NOT changed — this is a published library and they are applied in consumer files, so altering their geometry would restyle other people's work unannounced. Each now carries a description naming the elevation/* style that supersedes it and the exact divergence. Retire them only with evidence of zero consumers.

focus.note: Six `Focus States/*` effect styles. Unlike the shadows these are in GOOD shape — every one binds its colour to `color/transparent/<family>/48`, so they follow the brand and cannot rot into a literal. They shipped with no description at all, which is now fixed; each says which intent it belongs to and carries the geometry caveat below.
focus.geometryDivergence: Each style is a SINGLE FLUSH 4px spread. The build renders a 2px ring held 2px off the control (focus/width = ref/border/width/md = 2px, focus/offset = ref/space/xxs = 2px), so the total footprint agrees at 4px but the transparent gap does not exist in Figma. This is a LIMITATION, not drift to be fixed: a drop shadow cannot leave a transparent gap without painting the backdrop, and faking the gap means painting the inner 2px in the page colour — correct on the default surface and wrong on every other. Do not 'correct' these to two layers; the Figma ring is deliberately the heavier reading of the same affordance.

styles.Focus States/Primary - Active Shadow: bound to color/transparent/primary/48 — same value as the focus/ring token; the estate default

$valueChecksums.note: Per-collection checksum over `name|mode|value`, computed by build/figma-value-parity.mjs. The rest of this file records NAMES, and every check built on it compares names — which is why the library could hold 13 component tokens bound to the wrong palette rung, a reverted webfont, and 54 fluid-type variables carrying the old tablet curve, all under the correct names, with nothing noticing. `payload` is what the build produces; `figmaObserved` is a verified read of the library. They are expected to be EQUAL, and figma-value-parity.test.mjs fails when the payload moves without this record being refreshed.

knownDifference.$note: Re-verified 2026-08-14 against a LIVE read of the library, not against the previous record. Every difference below is stated with its exact arithmetic in BOTH directions. An observed value must come from a read; where it merely mirrors the payload it is an assumption wearing the costume of evidence. The direction that matters is payload-only: a library-only variable is an orphan the code stopped defining, but a PAYLOAD-ONLY variable is code defining something the library has no name for.
